Zihan found out the week her Indonesian recitation won the provincial cup and her grandfather Wira's back room in Chengdu filled with cousins asking her to say something, anything. Zihan noticed he no longer corrected her in front of anyone. On the mornings after the cousins visited, a few words appeared at the edge of the table, faint, in that same blue, gone by noon. For eleven years she had rented the corner room of the Lyon cooperative from him, and for nine the walnut shuttle he had lent her, the winter her own cracked, had crossed her warp thousands of times a day. A new shuttle, bought that spring, still lay in its paper in a drawer. Lucien picked it up, weighed it, and set it down. He walked to the shelf where her finished bolts were stacked and ran his thumb along an edge; every length carried the same faint ridge, a catch in the weave that no other loom in the building made. Buyers now asked for it by name. He said, mostly to the window, that the shuttle had learned her hand better than it had ever learned his. Imtiaz offered to return it after the current order. g.passage: Gyms remember everything. Caoimhe thought so as she sat on the low bench in the Glasgow school gym beside Jianguo, her stepson of eight months, while the deputy head read the janitor's account aloud: the boy seen at the equipment cupboard at four, the hasp forced by ten past. Jianguo spun a basketball on one finger. Caoimhe asked whether the janitor's watch had been checked against the bell, whether the hasp had been loose before, who else held keys. Each question came out clipped and orderly, and she wrote the answers in her diary as though preparing for a hearing. Then the deputy turned a page. A first-year's mother had phoned: Jianguo had sat with her son in the library until half four, going over fractions. The ball slowed and dropped into his lap. Caoimhe closed the diary. She tried to remember whether he had ever told her about the library, and could not, and found that the question she wanted to ask now was not one for the deputy. g.passage: Grapes have no business in Galway. Rory grows them anyway along the south wall of his workshop, and each October he presses them in a press he built before you, Aoife, became his apprentice. This year the press splits along one cheek. Rory has a glue for such repairs, made from a recipe he has never written down; for three years you have asked for it and been told you will learn it when you need it. He mixes it now while you watch, measuring nothing, talking about the weather. When you reach for a pencil, he sends you to the shed for clamps. g.passage: What is owed to someone who leaves without a word and returns the same way? I turned that over at the bus depot in Gdansk, where my brother Marcus and I waited for our cousin Zofia, eleven years after she had boarded a night coach to Berlin. Marcus had polished his shoes and rehearsed, in the van, how the radio shop could use another pair of hands. I had rehearsed something sharper. She stepped down with one small bag, thinner than I remembered, kissed us both, and explained nothing. On the drive home she asked about every customer she could still name. g.passage: A clay jar, cracked through, rested on the floor of the salt-water pool in Colombo, where Alonso had dropped it showing off for the fishermen's boys.
